kind: state and honesty: two balls start at one point, and the assumptions promise what the program does not do
request: compare learning rate 0.1 and 1.5 on the same surface

review.note: the draft the reviewer judged, as the model wrote it (the host seals it); verified for the mixed-arrow-scales job by re-sealing (the hash of the sealed draft equals the review's artifactHash), for the others by the job's recorded draft-hash chain

whyItMustFail: Two walkers start at exactly the same point and size, so one hides the other before any step (the comparison the request asks for cannot be seen), and the assumptions say an off-square ball is drawn at the surface edge height while the program places it at its true off-square position. Both are authored: a layout and a claim the computation does not make.

knownFindings.message: At the initial state both balls sit at exactly the same point, so the orange ball completely hides the blue one. The learner sees one ball, but the description promises two. Make both visible at the start, for example by drawing the blue ball slightly larger as a ring or halo, adding a shared start marker with a 'Blue 0.1 / Orange 1.5' tag, or offsetting the two balls a little.
knownFindings.c9Why: both balls start at one point: authored layout

knownFindings.message: The 'Minimum' label sits just below the minimum dot, which is exactly where the blue ball settles and the orange zig-zag segments cross. It covers path segments and crowds the blue ball. Move the label off to the side or the back of the bowl (or put it on a leader line), so the convergence region stays clear.
knownFindings.c9Renderer: may be eased by the C9 renderer
knownFindings.c9Why: a label placed over crossing paths is partly the declutter, which is renderer

knownFindings.message: The assumptions say a ball that leaves the square is 'drawn at the surface edge height'. The program does not do this. pos() places the ball at its true off-square position (here y≈4.66, beyond the edge) at height K·L+R, so orange floats outside the bowl, away from the edge. Either clamp the drawn position to the square's boundary at the edge height, or correct the text.
knownFindings.c9Why: the assumption and the program disagree: authored

knownFindings.message: At lrA=2 the blue ball diverges to (−3, 8), twice the square's half-width. It is drawn far off the bowl and floats in the air (height clamped by the host). This contradicts the stated 'drawn at the surface edge height', and it pulls the fitted camera out so the bowl shrinks. Clamp the drawn position of an off-square ball to the boundary.
knownFindings.c9Why: the program draws the ball at its true off-square position; the host clamps height only

knownFindings.message: Because of the far-off blue ball, the bowl and both zig-zags occupy a smaller part of the frame. The 'Minimum' label again sits over the crossing paths near the centre.
knownFindings.c9Renderer: may be eased by the C9 renderer
knownFindings.c9Why: framing of a far-off ball and a label over crossing paths are renderer

knownFindings.message: The side view confirms that only the orange ball is visible at the start. The blue ball is hidden inside it.
knownFindings.c9Why: the blue ball is hidden inside the orange one at the start: authored layout

knownFindings.message: The orange ball floats beyond the bowl's edge after it leaves the square. It is not placed at the edge as the assumptions claim.
knownFindings.c9Why: the program places the orange ball beyond the edge; the assumption says at the edge

knownFindings.message: The diverged blue ball and its last path segment hang in mid-air well outside the surface, and the long blue segment passes over the bowl. This reads as a part floating in 3D. Placing off-square balls at the boundary would fix it.
knownFindings.c9Why: the program draws the diverged ball in mid-air outside the surface

plan.title: Learning rate 0.1 vs 1.5: gradient descent on the same bowl
plan.description: A stretched bowl-shaped loss surface with contour lines holds two marker balls that start from the same point. The blue ball uses learning rate 0.1 and the orange ball uses 1.5. On each step, both balls jump in the downhill direction. The jump is the learning rate times the slope (the gradient), and each ball leaves a path. Blue creeps smoothly toward the bottom, while orange overshoots and zig-zags across the narrow valley in wider and wider swings until it leaves the surface.
plan.reason: With both learning rates on one surface and one starting point, any difference in their paths comes only from the learning rate. You can play, pause or step to watch it happen, then change either rate to find where steady progress turns into overshooting.
interactions: Play, pause or step: each step moves both balls once, and the paths grow behind them.
Change either learning rate. Both balls go back to the start point and their paths clear, so you can see the new behavior from the beginning.
Move the shared start point to see whether the comparison still holds from another place on the surface.
Clear both paths and send both balls back to the start point, keeping your current settings.
Read each ball's step count, current loss and status (going down, settled, or left the surface).
assumptions: Illustration: a made-up bowl formula, not the loss of a real trained model.

The loss is 0.5·x² + 0.75·y² on a square from −4 to 4. Its curvature is 1 along the long direction and 1.5 along the narrow one, and the surface is drawn with its height scaled down so it fits the view.
Each step is plain gradient descent with no momentum or noise: new position = old position − learning rate × slope. The exact slope from the formula is used.
Each ball stops when its loss drops below 0.001 (settled), when it moves off the square (shown as left the surface, meaning it diverged), or after 60 steps.
limitations: Along each direction, a step multiplies the distance to the bottom by 1 − learning rate × curvature. In the narrow direction, rates from 0.67 to 1.33 swing back and forth but still shrink. Above 1.33 the swings grow.
In the long direction, swings grow only above 2, so that never happens within the slider range. These thresholds belong to this bowl only. Other surfaces have different safe ranges.

At 1.5 the orange ball still closes in along the long direction, swinging past the bottom each step. Its distance in the narrow direction grows by 1.25 times per step, so it leaves the surface after roughly 10 steps from the default start.
A real loss surface is bumpier and has more than two directions. This bowl shows the core effect of step size, not every behavior of real training.
plan.learningGoal: See that a small learning rate makes slow, steady progress downhill, while a learning rate too large for the surface's steepest curve overshoots the bottom and can swing farther away each step.

draft.title: Learning rate 0.1 vs 1.5 on one loss bowl
draft.description: A stretched bowl-shaped loss surface with contour lines, 8 by 8 units, lowest at the centre. Two balls start at the same point. Blue uses one learning rate (default 0.1), orange another (default 1.5). Each step, both move by minus their learning rate times the slope and leave a path. Blue creeps steadily to the bottom. Orange zig-zags across the narrow direction with growing swings until it leaves the surface. Readouts show each ball's loss, status and step count.
assumptions: Illustration: a made-up bowl formula, not the loss of a real trained model.

Loss = 0.5·x² + 0.75·y² on the square −4 to 4 (x long direction left-right, y narrow direction front-back). Curvature is 1 along x and 1.5 along y. The surface is drawn at 0.15 times the loss so it fits the view.
Each step is plain gradient descent, no momentum or noise: new position = old − learning rate × exact slope. While running, both balls take 5 steps per second.
A ball stops when its loss drops below 0.001 (settled), when it moves off the square (left the surface, meaning it diverged; it is then drawn at the surface edge height), or after 60 steps.

Each step multiplies the distance to the bottom by 1 − rate × curvature. Along y, rates from 0.67 to 1.33 swing but shrink, and rates above 1.33 make the swings grow. Along x, swings would only grow above 2, which is outside the slider range.

At 1.5, orange's y distance grows 1.25 times per step, so from the default start it leaves after 10 steps. Blue at 0.1 settles after about 40 steps. Changing any setting sends both balls back to the start and clears their paths.
A real loss surface is bumpier and has many more directions. This bowl shows the core effect of step size only.
